question: The major focus of my recent travels has been visiting all of the UNESCO World Heritage sites. When I visit a new country, I feel like it helps me appreciate where I am staying for more than just a few popular sites I have seen on social media. I have been paying special attention to what they call "The List in Danger," and I like to prioritize those locations if possible. I have recently visited Cameroon and Chad, and I think that my next destination will be the Democratic Republic of the Congo in June 2025. While I am there, it is my dream to see a Kordofan giraffe. Where could I see them when I visit?

**Where you can see a Kordofan giraffe in the Democratic Republic of Congo** | Feature | Details | |---------|---------| | **Location** | **Garamba National Park** – Haut‑Uélé Province, Northeast DRC (≈ 3°30′ N, 28°30′ E) | | **UNESCO status** | World Heritage Site (inscribed 1980) – not on “List in Danger” | | **Giraffe subspecies** | *Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum* (Kordofan giraffe) – the only remaining population in the DRC | | **Population** | ~ 80–110 individuals as of 2024, steadily increasing due to anti‑poaching and monitoring programmes | | **Other wildlife** | Forest elephants, hippos, lions, buffalo, aerial‑borne “shoebill” storks, etc. | | **Access** | - **By air**: flight from Goma to Nagero (park airstrip) or charter from Kinshasa/[Bangui](https://www.bangui.org).
- **By road**: 10‑15 h from Goma via the “Fizi” route (recommended only with experienced guide).
- **Entrance fee**: ₲ 10 000 000 (~US$ 10–12) for foreign visitors (prices change; confirm with tour operator). | | **Recommended tour operators** | - **African Parks**: runs ranger‑led game drives and monitor‑based safari packages.
- **DRC Tourism**: licensed guides and airport transfers.
- **Local safari companies**: offer 5‑ to 7‑day itineraries focussed on giraffe viewing. | | **Best time to visit** | • **Dry season** (Jan – March & Sept – Nov): visibility is good, animals are easier to spot;
• **Wet season** (Jun – Aug): park gets very lush, but some roads become muddy – still possible with a charter;
| **Why Garamba?** The Kordofan giraffe has survived only in Garamba National Park. Surveys conducted by **African Parks** + the **Giraffe Conservation Foundation (GCF)** confirmed that the park’s sub‑species population is the **last in Africa**—the species that used to live across Central and West Africa is now confined here alone (GiraffeConservation.org). > *"Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country."*【source: 10, 11】 Because the park is the **sole refuge**, visiting it is the **only way** to see a Kordofan giraffe in person. > *"The last remaining population of Critically Endangered Kordofan giraffe in the DRC continues to grow steadily."*【source: 5】 **How to maximise your chances** 1. **Go with a ranger‑led tour.** Guided game‑drives in the park’s “open savannah zones” (north sector) yield the highest giraffe encounter rates. 2. **Arrive at least 2 days early** to acclimatise, clear licences, and pick the right season. 3. **Use real‑time GPS tracking** (available via the park’s management system) to join the “giraffe circuit” that follows the most active herds. 4. **Plan for extra fuel and water**—the park’s internal roads can be treacherous, especially during rains. **Practical considerations for June 2025** * **June falls into the rainy season** (generally short bursts). Roads may become slippery, but air transport to Nagero is reliable. * **African Parks’ maintain a constant anti‑poaching patrol** and have a dedicated staff for visitors, so the park remains safe even during the rains. * **Carry insect repellent** and a **rain jacket** – the park’s canopy is dense and humid at the start of the wet season. **Extra tip: “List in Danger” context** While you are prioritising UNESCO sites that are threatened, Garamba itself is *not* on the UNESCO “List in Danger.” However, the park’s *Kordofan giraffe* is critically endangered (IUCN status = Critically Endangered). Visiting Garamba therefore aligns with both goals: you see a World Heritage site and help support the survival of a critically endangered subspecies. --- ### Bottom line **If you want to see a Kordofan giraffe in June 2025, schedule a visit to Garamba National Park.** A Botswana‑style “giraffe safari” with African Parks or a locally‑licensed guide will give you the best chance of spotting these rare giants, while also letting you experience one of the DRC’s most spectacular—and historically significant—national parks.

# Kordofan Giraffe Conservation in DRC
Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country. Despite threats from poaching and rebel activities, GCF, African Parks, and the DRC government have successfully achieved a steady increase in giraffe numbers.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

Good news from DRC!
Garamba National Park is home to the only giraffe population  in the country.
With GCF's support, our partners at African Parks keep a close eye on these critically endangered Kordofan giraffe  during regular aerial  and ground patrols. The current population stands at 92 known individuals including 5 new  giraffe that were observed for the first time in recent months.
After decades of civil unrest with related poaching and habitat destruction, and despite ongoing challenges, this important  giraffe population is gradually recovering.

## Where to See Kordofan Giraffes in DRC — Complete Safari Guide
Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is home to critically endangered Kordofan giraffes, forest elephants, hippos, and lions — one of Africa's oldest and most exclusive national parks, managed by African Parks with zero tourist crowds.
Quick Answer
**Yes, there are giraffes in the DRC.** Garamba National Park hosts Kordofan giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum) — one of the rarest giraffe subspecies. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site established in 1938, covering 4,902 km² in northeast DRC's Haut-Uélé Province.

## Kordofan Giraffes — Congo's Rarest Giants
The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is one of the most endangered giraffe subspecies in the world, with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in the wild. Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is one of its last strongholds.
Distinguished by their paler coloring and irregular patches that extend further down their legs compared to other subspecies, Kordofan giraffes were once widespread across Central and West Africa. Today, their range has collapsed dramatically.
African Parks, in partnership with ICCN (Congo's wildlife authority), has significantly improved the park's security and infrastructure since 2005, creating conditions for wildlife recovery and limited but growing tourism access.

# Kordofan Giraffe Conservation in DRC
Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country. Despite threats from poaching and rebel activities, GCF, African Parks, and the DRC government have successfully achieved a steady increase in giraffe numbers.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

## Where to See Kordofan Giraffes in DRC — Complete Safari Guide
Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is home to critically endangered Kordofan giraffes, forest elephants, hippos, and lions — one of Africa's oldest and most exclusive national parks, managed by African Parks with zero tourist crowds.
Quick Answer
**Yes, there are giraffes in the DRC.** Garamba National Park hosts Kordofan giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum) — one of the rarest giraffe subspecies. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site established in 1938, covering 4,902 km² in northeast DRC's Haut-Uélé Province.

## Kordofan Giraffes — Congo's Rarest Giants
The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is one of the most endangered giraffe subspecies in the world, with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in the wild. Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is one of its last strongholds.
Distinguished by their paler coloring and irregular patches that extend further down their legs compared to other subspecies, Kordofan giraffes were once widespread across Central and West Africa. Today, their range has collapsed dramatically.
African Parks, in partnership with ICCN (Congo's wildlife authority), has significantly improved the park's security and infrastructure since 2005, creating conditions for wildlife recovery and limited but growing tourism access.

| **Why Garamba?** The Kordofan giraffe has survived only in Garamba National Park. Surveys conducted by **African Parks** + the **Giraffe Conservation Foundation (GCF)** confirmed that the park’s sub‑species population is the **last in Africa**—the species that used to live across Central and West Africa is now confined here alone (GiraffeConservation.org). > *"Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country."*【source: 10, 11】 Because the park is the **sole refuge**, visiting it is the **only way** to see a Kordofan giraffe in person. > *"The last remaining population of Critically Endangered Kordofan giraffe in the DRC continues to grow steadily."*【source: 5】 **How to maximise your chances** 1. **Go with a ranger‑led tour.** Guided game‑drives in the park’s “open savannah zones” (north sector) yield the highest giraffe encounter rates. 2. **Arrive at least 2 days early** to acclimatise, clear licences, and pick the right season. 3. **Use real‑time GPS tracking** (available via the park’s management system) to join the “giraffe circuit” that follows the most active herds. 4. **Plan for extra fuel and water**—the park’s internal roads can be treacherous, especially during rains. **Practical considerations for June 2025** * **June falls into the rainy season** (generally short bursts).
